newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel for clear EMU stability pact, no jobs link.
newsitem.headline: Waigel for clear EMU stability pact, no jobs link.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel stuck to his strict line on Europe's planned single currency on Thursday, saying it had to be flanked by clear penalties for profligate members with as little leeway as possible.

Speaking only hours before a special ECOFIN meeting meant to smooth the way for the European Union summit Dublin on Friday, Waigel said he would not be swayed from his widely criticised stand on a strict stability pact for the euro.
He also rebuffed calls in Germany and abroad for the European Union to launch a massive drive to create jobs, saying this challenge had to be met at the national level.

"I will not move away from the clear stability goal," Waigel said. "Every member state must know what the consequences are if it diverges from the stability path and lets its budget deficit go over three percent.
"The community procedure that then sets in must be transparent and unequivocal," he said, adding the pact needed "verifiable definitions" of allowable exceptions so it could be applied effectively.
"Exceptions because of natural catastrophes or a strong economic downturn that justify going over the three percent limit must be defined as narrowly as possible," he said.

Waigel, who has been criticised in the EU for trying to shut politicial decision-making out of this penalty procedure as much as possible, avoided using the word "automatic" that has irritated his critics, especially in France.

"We don't want all decisions on economic, budgetary, fiscal and monetary policy to be shaped by a technocratic, automatic system under the sole authority of the ECB (European Central Bank)," French Prime Minister Alain Juppe told the Financial Times on Monday. "That is not our concept of democracy."
Waigel said the European jobs programme plan championed by the left-wing opposition in Germany and France would be a failure.
"It would only cost German taxpayers money and its success is highly doubtful," he said.

Waigel also said Germany's overall public sector deficit from federal, state and local governments would be 2.5 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, the crucial year for qualifying for the single currency.
